# Embarrassingly Simple Access Control for Large Language Models

[All reading notes](../reading-notes.md) · [Catalog entry](../README.md#access-control-probes)

**Full paper read · 2026-11-16**

[Original source](https://aclanthology.org/2026.aacl-long.110.pdf) · AACL-IJCNLP 2026 proceedings, pages 2417–2431, 6–10 November 2026

**Reading coverage:** All 15 PDF pages: Sections 1–7, limitations, references, Appendices A–F, role/policy examples, normal and adversarial prompts, hyperparameters, both workflow figures and Tables 1–8. Tables 3 and 5–7 were additionally inspected visually on PDF pages 6 and 8. Author publication metadata and public artifact discovery were checked separately.

## Research question

Natural-language database requests may be answerable but disallowed for a particular role, and prompting alone can miss restrictions in long table/column policies.

## Method

Combines role, policy and query text, extracts the final token's last-layer hidden state from frozen Llama, Qwen or Mistral models, and fits a logistic-regression authorization probe. Separate probes are learned for each model rather than changing the language-model weights.

## Evaluation

Uses RBAC-adapted BIRD/Spider and the organizational OrgAccess benchmark, database- or department-separated splits, multiple policy lengths, direct/two-step prompting comparators and adversarial instructions. Macro-F1 measures access-decision classification; the study does not evaluate end-to-end secure SQL execution.

## What the results support

Standard SQL-policy probes generally outperform matched prompting, particularly on long policies. These gains are model-dependent: adversarial instructions sharply reduce performance, and probes lose seven of nine matched OrgAccess comparisons. Best standard averages on BIRD and Spider come from different backbones.

## Limits and qualifications

Synthetic policy structures and small model families limit transfer. Prediction quality does not guarantee permission enforcement, calibrated false-permit risk or multi-turn robustness. The binary sigmoid/BCE description does not explain OrgAccess's three-label training/decoding, and the cross-dataset generalization paragraph lacks a complete dedicated results table. Implementation availability remains unverified.

## Relevance to reliable Text-to-SQL

Supplies a lightweight baseline and negative evidence for policy-based refusal gates, distinct from semantic answerability detection and SQL-generation correctness.
